name: Perm / texture perm

lead: A perm chemically reshapes hair into waves or curls, and texture perms use the same idea for volume and a wavy or curly look. The curl is visible at once and gives a fuller, more styled head of hair.

On looksmaxxing forums users describe it as a way to change facial framing, with some claiming a boost of about 1 PSL and a way to cover weaker eye-area features. No attractiveness studies of perms were found.

paras: A reducing agent such as thioglycolate breaks keratin disulfide bonds while hair is wrapped on rods, and a neutralizer, usually hydrogen peroxide, reforms them in the curled shape. Modern perms descend from the 1938 cold wave, and results grow out as new hair appears.
Chemical processing can irritate the scalp and damage hair, and related chemical relaxers are associated with burns, dermatitis, breakage and hair loss.

angle.text: Forum users get perms for added texture and volume, with posters describing a boost of about 1 PSL and a way to soften weaker eye-area features. The curl change is visible at once; no attractiveness research has tested the rating claims.

lead: A perm (permanent wave) is a chemical hairstyling procedure that reshapes hair into waves or curls by breaking and reforming the disulfide bonds in keratin. A reducing agent, classically ammonium thioglycolate, breaks the bonds while the hair is wrapped on rods, and a neutralizer such as hydrogen peroxide reforms them in the new shape.[1] A texture perm applies the same chemistry to add wave, curl, volume and movement to hair that is straight or flat.

People use perms to change how the hair frames the face. Added volume and curl alter the outline of the head, can add apparent height at the crown, and can fall across the forehead or brow area. On looksmaxxing forums, wavy and digital perms are discussed as a hair-based way to improve facial framing and overall look: some threads claim that a perm adds a point on the PSL scale, and others propose that perm styling can draw attention away from the eye area.[2][3][4]

Modern perms descend from the 1938 cold wave, which required no heat, after earlier thermal and electric methods in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries; types now include alkaline, acid, exothermic and digital perms.[1][5] Perms were a mass-market phenomenon in the 1970s and 1980s, and digital or hot perms have remained especially popular in East Asia.[1][5] No published clinical studies of perms and perceived attractiveness were found; the research that touches the topic concerns the chemistry of hair waving and the safety of related straightening products.[6]

paras: Hair's strength and elasticity come from disulfide bonds between keratin chains. In a perm, ammonium or sodium thioglycolate at a pH of about 8 to 9.5 breaks these bonds over roughly 15 to 30 minutes while the hair is wound, and a neutralizer then reforms them.[1] Acid perms, developed in the 1970s, use glyceryl monothioglycolate at a lower pH with added heat and are described as gentler on hair because the cuticle stays more closed.[1] Related chemistry without rods is used in permanent relaxers, which flatten rather than curl the hair; thio relaxers, for example, use ammonium thioglycolate at a pH above 10.[1][6]

Wikipedia's account of the procedure lists the typical steps: the hair is washed, cut and sectioned; it is wound on rods using either spiral (root-to-tip) or croquignole (tip-first) winding; the waving solution is applied; and an oxidizing neutralizer sets the new shape. Rod shape and size matter: straight and concave rods give different curls, and smaller rods produce tighter curls.[1] Spiral winding gives a three-dimensional curl, while croquignole winding gives a flatter, two-dimensional one.[1]

Alkaline or classic perms work at room temperature, usually with ammonium thioglycolate at pH 9 to 10, and are described as suiting coarser, stronger hair. Acid perms use glyceryl monothioglycolate at about pH 6.5 to 8.2 and are slower. Exothermic perms are self-heating and self-timing, and neutral or low-pH thioglycolate-free variants also exist.[1]

Soft, temporary and spot perms were later additions: spot perms target a small area such as a fringe or the ends, and self-neutralizing, no-mix and no-ammonia home formulations appeared after the home-kit boom.[1]

A digital perm uses hot rods whose temperature is controlled by a machine with a digital display, which is why stylists often call it a hot perm. It uses a different solution plus heat, whereas a normal cold perm uses a waving solution and a neutralizer.[5] The name 'digital perm' is trademarked by the Japanese company Paimore, and the technique is popular in several countries including South Korea and Japan.[1][5]

Wikipedia's article on the technique notes a visual difference: a cold perm looks most defined when the hair is wet and looser when dry, while a digital perm is the reverse, with the wave most prominent when the hair is dry. It adds that digital perms usually cost more and take longer than cold perms.[5]

sections.h: How people use perms to change their looks
paras: The appearance case for a perm rests on hair as a framing device. Waves and curls add width and volume around the head, can lift the crown, and give the hairline and fringe a different shape; on straight, fine or flat hair they supply texture that styling alone may not hold. Because the result lasts for months rather than until the next wash, it removes the daily styling step for people who want a consistent wavy or curly look.[1]

Forum users describe perms as part of 'hair maxxing', the set of hair-related changes (cut, colour, density, texture) discussed as improving overall appearance. In these threads the perm is presented as especially useful for people whose hair is straight and who want movement and volume, and for people who want hair to cover or soften particular areas of the face.[2][3][4]

Marcel Grateau created a practical thermal waving method with heated tongs in 1872; it produced flat waves and could damage hair.[1] On 8 October 1905 German hairdresser Karl Nessler demonstrated an electric spiral-heat method using caustic soda that took about six hours, and his early attempts burned his wife's hair; he later worked in London and the United States, opening salons in several American cities.[1] In 1917 Isidoro Calvete designed a practical heater for Eugene Suter, whose firm Eugene Ltd. became synonymous with permanent waving, and around 1924 Josef Mayer is credited with point-winding.[1] In 1928 Marjorie Joyner received a patent for a permanent wave machine, the first awarded to an African American woman.[1]

Chemistry replaced heat in the 1930s. Sulfur-based reducing agents were introduced around 1930, and in 1931 Ralph Evans and Everett McDonough showed a heatless 'overnight wave' at a Chicago beauty show. Arnold Willatt developed the cold wave in 1938, using ammonium thioglycolate and hydrogen peroxide over a process that originally took many hours.[1] The Second World War halted European production of perming equipment.[1]

Home perm kits made the procedure a household product. TONI, made by the Toni Home Permanent Company of Minnesota in the 1940s and 1950s, advertised with twins, one with a salon perm and one with a home perm; Lilt from Procter & Gamble and the British brand Twink followed.[1] Home perms peaked in the 1970s and 1980s, and demand has since declined in many markets.[1] Acid perms arrived in the 1970s, and the 21st century brought digital perms.[1][5]

On looksmax.org perms appear in threads about hair, ascension and fixing a bad result. One thread titled in terms of a wavy perm giving a one-point PSL boost, and another pairing a perm with a 'down perm', put the claim in numerical terms; a user in the latter asks how to obtain a digital perm abroad, describing hair as the one remaining thing holding back their improvement.[2][4] Another thread proposes that someone with a good lower third and weaker eyes can cover the eyes with perm styling.[3] Further threads are titled around a digital perm being a 'halo' and around whether the poster should get a perm.[7][8]

The community also discusses getting a similar look without chemicals. One thread asks how to make straighter hair wavier without a perm, and a reply recommends a thick leave-in conditioner on damp hair and a scrunching technique, while other threads ask how to go from wavy to curly hair or have curly hair without a perm.[9][10] A further thread asks how to fix a perm that has grown out for a month, with one reply suggesting buzzing the hair.[11]

Wikipedia notes that early heat-based methods could burn hair and scalp and carried shock or scalding hazards.[1] Chemical relaxers using related chemistry are associated with scalp burns, dermatitis, breakage and hair loss, and lye relaxers typically contain 5 to 10 percent sodium hydroxide at pH 10 to 14.[6] In the 1990s the Rio Hair Naturalizer System, marketed as chemical-free, was linked to scalp damage and hair loss and led to a class action; the product was withdrawn.[6]

Epidemiological studies of straightening products, including an NIH-AARP analysis of more than 33,000 women reporting an association between frequent use and roughly doubled uterine cancer risk, concern relaxers and straighteners rather than wave perms specifically; researchers say further work is needed.[6] Regulators have taken action on some straightening products: the US FDA proposed banning formaldehyde as a hair-relaxer ingredient in 2023.[6] Cosmetics in the US are not subject to pre-market FDA approval.[6]

Hairdressing sources describe acid and low-pH perms as gentler on the cuticle than classic alkaline perms.[1] Hair that has been chemically processed regrows untreated at the roots, so curls grow out with new hair over several months.[1]

Related hair-texture procedures include chemical relaxers and straighteners, which reverse the curl chemistry, and non-chemical routes to wave such as heatless styling products and conditioner-based curl routines discussed in the community threads above.[6][9] Perms sit alongside cut, colour and density work in the broader hair-maxxing toolkit.
No studies of perms and perceived attractiveness were found. Studies of the safety of related chemical straighteners are described under Risks.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, perms are discussed as a way to improve overall appearance through hair, with threads on wavy and digital perms, on getting curl without a perm, and on perm aftercare.[2][3][4][9]
